title: Organised crime: better intelligence, stronger local policing and the limits of current plans
label: 18 November 2026 · Organised crime and local communities
summary: The committee questioned the Home Office about how organised crime is changing, including criminal activity in high-street shops, rural areas and online. Sarah Jones said police need better shared information, stronger neighbourhood policing and a reformed national structure, while acknowledging that plans and evidence are still developing. Members challenged the Government on police staffing, the lack of dedicated funding for some successful local approaches, uneven support for rural areas, and whether enforcement alone can reduce drug harm.

glossary.definition: The National Crime Agency, which investigates serious and organised crime and works with police and other agencies.
A local crime-fighting approach: remove criminal activity, stop it returning, then work with partners to improve the area.
Regional organised crime units that tackle serious crime across several local police areas.
Detailed rules made by ministers under powers given to them by an Act of Parliament.
A UK law that requires online services to take steps to deal with illegal content and other online harms.
Court orders requiring people convicted of crime to give up money or property gained through crime.

chapters.title: Changing crime and the need for local intelligence
chapters.takeaway: Criminals adapt quickly, so the Home Office says police need better shared data and stronger local knowledge.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: Where are the biggest gaps in what the Government know about serious and organised crime, and how will you improve the national picture?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The threat keeps changing, particularly as criminals use new technology. The NCA collects information from police, surveys and other sources, then prioritises action according to the likely danger and harm.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: But there are areas we still understand poorly. Criminals are using struggling high streets, including some vape shops, to carry out several kinds of crime. We’re only beginning to understand how the groups involved connect.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: A committee visit showed how technology can bring together information from many sources. Are we investing enough in the right tools, and can useful intelligence reach officers dealing with a problem on the street?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Police systems are old and often don’t work well together. We’re investing in them so information can be analysed, including with artificial intelligence, but the data has to be made usable first.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Technology is also needed to find new forms of drug smuggling. Criminals can change drugs into other products or leave them underwater with location trackers. The NCA is investing in upgrading its technology.

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: The NCA has a budget close to £1.1 billion this year, up 19% on 2024-25. A significant part of the increase is for its technology.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: For illegal shops, the answer also has to be agencies working together in person: police, trading standards, the tax authority and Companies House. The difficulty is making that kind of information-sharing work across all crime, not just one programme.

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: National teams that spot patterns across local areas have helped with different crime types. They can then pass what they learn back to local police, who can act on it.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: The public still feel unsafe even when some crime figures are falling. Why?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: People see shop theft, antisocial behaviour and suspicious shops on their high streets. Those everyday crimes affect how safe people feel, and years of reduced neighbourhood policing have left a real gap.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’ve also heard that forced labour can occur throughout supply chains. When you change policy, for example on vape packaging, do you assess whether it could increase or reduce exploitation?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We can take that question away.

chapters.title: Neighbourhood policing and police reform
chapters.takeaway: The Minister backed more neighbourhood policing but could not say how many planned officers are new recruits rather than officers moved from other jobs.

turns.speaker: Matt Bishop
turns.text: Neighbourhood police numbers have risen, but the overall police workforce has fallen. Was that intended, and where are the extra neighbourhood officers coming from?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The old funding rules encouraged forces to keep officer numbers up even when it meant moving officers into office jobs and cutting police staff. We’ve given chiefs more freedom to decide what roles they need.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Some neighbourhood officers are new recruits; others are moved from different roles. By next year, we expect nearly 5,000 more people in neighbourhood policing, against a target of 13,000. There are about 20,900 now, but we don’t have a breakdown of how many are new.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: If officers are moved into neighbourhood work, what happens to their old jobs? Forces have warned that community engagement, traffic policing and intelligence gathering could suffer.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re collecting more information on force performance and would be surprised if other services were harmed. Chiefs are responsible for managing their staff, and we’ll monitor the results. Overall police numbers have gone down, though.

turns.speaker: Matt Bishop
turns.text: Can technology reduce the time officers spend on paperwork? And how will you make sure neighbourhood policing doesn’t come at the expense of investigations or emergency response?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We think new tools could free up time equivalent to 3,000 officers by the end of this Parliament, including by reducing form-filling and speeding up the handling of evidence. But neighbourhood work, response and investigations can’t be treated as an either-or choice.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re also setting clearer limits on when neighbourhood officers can be taken away for other duties. Local commands should protect neighbourhood policing, response and everyday crime work.

turns.speaker: Matt Bishop
turns.text: Will neighbourhood officers be trained to investigate, and will they gain experience doing the job on the streets?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Investigation is part of all six areas of the new neighbourhood training. The College of Policing is also preparing the first professional guidance for neighbourhood policing. And yes, frontline experience matters.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Clear, Hold, Build has been linked to a roughly 23% reduction in theft and other property crime. Why isn’t the Government funding it, and must every force use it?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The Home Office hasn’t funded the approach, including during its trial. We generally give money to local forces and let them choose how to use it. The results are encouraging, but I haven’t told every force it must use it.

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: It depends on the area and on whether councils and community groups are involved. It has worked well in some medium-sized neighbourhoods, but it’s intensive and can’t simply be applied everywhere.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The difficult part is often the long-term work to rebuild a community after crime is cleared. Are you considering funding that longer stage?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We haven’t decided what will be in the next spending bid. Rebuilding an area takes sustained work and investment, whether that’s helping young people avoid crime or bringing viable businesses back to a high street.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The wider reform plan is for a national police service, around 200 local policing areas and specialist teams between them. The exact boundaries aren’t settled. We want local commanders and named officers, but local policing mustn’t lose out as national structures change.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Devon and Cornwall officers worry that large cities could get priority over rural towns. How will the new boundaries reflect rural travel, seasonal demand and local geography?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Those are live questions. We’re reviewing the funding formula, including whether it reflects rurality, deprivation and seasonal pressures. Local police commands must remain understandable and connected to their communities.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: Will each local area have senior, experienced police leadership rather than being left to more junior officers?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: I agree that local areas need proper commanders, clear standards and ways for residents and councils to scrutinise what police do. The exact size and boundaries of those areas are still being worked out.

chapters.title: High-street crime and enforcement
chapters.takeaway: The Government has funded raids and enforcement, but members questioned whether it can stop criminal shops reopening or support places left out of the main funding areas.

turns.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
turns.text: Operation Machinize visited or raided more than 3,000 premises. What happened after the arrests, and what else was seized?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: I don’t have the figures for charges. The operation seized £2.2 million in cash, froze £3.7 million in accounts, identified £4.2 million in tax evasion and seized £6.8 million in other assets.

turns.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
turns.text: If a shop closes and the same people open elsewhere, how will the new council and police know? How much of the £30 million goes to local trading standards?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re still developing the programme. We need to go beyond raiding individual shops and identify the gangs behind them, while making it harder for them to set up in the first place. £6 million is for trading standards and £20 million for the NCA and wider law enforcement, with some support for other agencies.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re looking at stronger powers for local authorities to stop unsuitable shops opening, and at whether sellers of vapes and illicit tobacco should need a licence. A ministerial group oversees the work, but we don’t yet have a target for the number of shops to close.

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: We’re trying to measure lasting results, not just how many raids we carry out. That means identifying the groups behind the shops and using measures such as longer closure orders.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The main target areas are the West Midlands, Greater Manchester, and Kent and Essex, based on intelligence about where the risk is greatest. Other forces can ask the NCA for support.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: West Yorkshire has had 20 raids in Keighley and more than 3,000 reports about suspicious shops, yet it wasn’t named as a main target. That gives my constituents little reassurance.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The areas were chosen using intelligence about where the greatest harm was judged to be. West Yorkshire can still seek support, and police and local agencies can carry out their own operations. I’ll check what the trading standards funding means for the area.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Raids don’t address professional services or financial institutions that may help criminal businesses operate. What are you doing to stop that support and to rebuild under-resourced trading standards teams?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: You’re right that we need to act earlier and share information held by different agencies. Local trading standards teams have lost capacity over many years, and rebuilding it is difficult. We’re also changing the law so authorities can close a shop for up to a year.

chapters.title: Rural crime and regional cooperation
chapters.takeaway: The Minister pointed to local policing and national operations as key tools, while members pressed her on the limited national funding for rural crime.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Rural crime can fall between national units and local police. Are you treating it as a specific priority?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Yes. Crime data is usually organised by type, not by whether it happened in a rural area, which can make patterns harder to see. National operations have helped tackle problems such as waste crime, equipment theft and hare coursing.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Local rural crime teams and officers who understand the area are important too. In places where farmers trust police and report crimes, forces can do a much better job.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: The national rural crime unit received £800,000. Is that enough when rural areas can be expensive to cover, and does the force funding formula properly account for rurality?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Most rural policing is paid for from force budgets, and chiefs decide how to spend that money. The national unit gets £800,000, and I think it provides good value. We want reforms to make effective practice more consistent between forces.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: How will the waste crime crackdown work with rural police, and is there new money for it?

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: There’s £45 million over three years for the Environment Agency to tackle waste sites. Police and the NCA support its work, and a national joint team is tackling serious organised waste crime. That approach is also being tried in Greater Manchester and West Yorkshire.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The Government’s equipment theft law still needs detailed rules before it can take full effect. Legal and practical issues around vehicle registration and manufacturers have delayed them. I hope we can bring them forward early next year.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: Why have immobilisers been dropped from the plans? These vehicles are often stolen by organised criminals.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re still working through what manufacturers can provide and what the law allows. I want to move quickly, but we also need a workable system for manufacturers and buyers.

turns.speaker: Robbie Moore
turns.text: How will the regional units fit into police reform without losing their expertise or support for local forces?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Those units do good work, but their funding and staffing arrangements are fragile: local forces pay for them and lend them officers. We want a more reliable structure, with national work in the national police service and regional specialisms in the new system.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We plan to build the national service gradually and only transfer major responsibilities when it can handle them. The aim is to improve both local policing and the national response to complex crime, without damaging work that already succeeds.

chapters.title: Drug supply, treatment and asset recovery
chapters.takeaway: The Government plans to update its drug strategy rather than make a radical change, while members questioned whether enforcement and treatment are reducing demand and crime.

turns.speaker: Preet Kaur Gill
turns.text: What does the review of the drug strategy involve, and when will it be published?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The earlier strategy’s focus on reducing demand and supply and improving treatment still makes sense. We’re reviewing what has changed: cocaine supply is growing, new synthetic drugs are appearing, and ketamine use has increased. We also need to know whether treatment is reaching the right people and helping them.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re looking at treatment for people who repeatedly steal, and at the links between drugs and rough sleeping. I hope we can set out the updated priorities before the end of the year.

turns.speaker: Mr Paul Kohler
turns.text: The strategy aimed to reduce demand and supply as well as improve treatment. Demand and the quantity of drugs available seem to have gone the wrong way. How far will you reconsider the approach?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: There isn’t a radical change planned, and we’re not proposing to legalise drugs. We want to update the strategy, improve how we judge treatment, and focus on the changing risks, including drugs sold online and the links between drug use and violence against women.

turns.speaker: Mr Paul Kohler
turns.text: Are you considering legalising or regulating cannabis, as some other countries have done?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: No. We’re not changing the law on cannabis. We’ll keep studying its harms, including the mental health effects.

turns.speaker: Dr Peter Prinsley
turns.text: You can’t arrest your way out of drug use. What are health and education departments doing to prevent it and explain the harm to young people?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: There has been a public campaign about ketamine and its serious effects on the bladder, and schools do drug education. I’d like to do more public health campaigns because many people don’t connect buying drugs with the harm they cause in communities and overseas.

turns.speaker: Ben Maguire
turns.text: Are you learning from other countries about screening luggage at ports and airports to stop drugs entering the UK?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: The NCA works closely with ports, but drugs are increasingly hidden in forms that existing detection methods may not find. We’re working to use better technology, though this is still a work in progress.

turns.speaker: Mr Paul Kohler
turns.text: Only a tiny share of criminal assets may be recovered. What is the Government doing to improve that?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We recovered about £345 million last year. A new strategy includes £550 million over three years to improve asset recovery, and letting local forces keep part of the money they recover gives them an incentive.

turns.speaker: Rod McLean
turns.text: The strategy also changes how confiscation orders are enforced, puts victims’ compensation first and aims to make court processes faster. Recovered assets rose 20% last year and are 57% higher than in 2020-21.

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: It’s becoming harder to trace money, especially when it’s moved through cryptocurrency or hidden in complex financial arrangements. The plan includes new powers to seize cryptocurrency and more financial investigators.

chapters.title: Crime and illegal sales online
chapters.takeaway: The Government is testing new ways to find stolen goods online but accepts that existing rules do not give it enough power over every kind of illegal sale.

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: What is the Home Office doing about illegal and counterfeit goods sold through social media and online marketplaces?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: We’re funding a tool that scans second-hand marketplaces for stolen goods. The Online Safety Act requires services to have plans to deal with illegal content, but we’re considering whether the rules go far enough.

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: Could online companies be forced to act on stolen or counterfeit goods in the same way they can be made to deal with illegal knife sales?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: There are stronger rules for knife sales, and companies or senior executives can face court action if they ignore them. For other illegal sales, companies must have plans and remove content when it is reported, but we don’t yet have the same tools to compel action.

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: Could the Government warn people, especially young people, that cheap counterfeit goods may fund crime and can also be unsafe?

turns.speaker: David Grahame
turns.text: Counterfeit goods can harm buyers as well as support criminal activity, because their contents and quality may be unsafe.

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: That’s worth considering. There’s more to do, including on drugs sold online and on helping people understand what they’re buying.

turns.speaker: Bell Ribeiro-Addy
turns.text: Will the online crime work cover other crimes too, such as child sexual exploitation?

turns.speaker: Sarah Jones MP
turns.text: Yes. Police use undercover methods to catch online abusers, but these crimes often cross borders and the scale of the problem remains very large.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want people to understand that a bargain that looks too good to be true may help fund criminal activity, forced labour and other harm.
